disease.inheritance: Autosomal dominant — CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in HTT exon 1 (≥40 repeats fully penetrant; 36-39 reduced penetrance)
disease.mechanism: Gain-of-function / toxic aggregate. The expanded CAG repeat encodes an abnormally long polyglutamine (polyQ) tract in the huntingtin N-terminus. Mutant huntingtin aggregates, disrupts proteostasis, and is toxic to striatal medium spiny neurons. Note: mutant huntingtin is also thought to lose some normal function (loss-of-function component), but the dominant disease driver is the toxic gain-of-function.
disease.autotac_rationale: ELIGIBLE. Mutant huntingtin is a toxic gain-of-function aggregate — a canonical target for selective degradation. Degrading mutant huntingtin (ideally allele-selectively, sparing wild-type huntingtin) is mechanistically appropriate. No degrader is yet approved; this is an active research frontier.
disease.prevalence: ~1 in 10,000 (Caucasian); ~30,000 symptomatic in US — commonly cited; UNVERIFIED exact figure this session
disease.age_of_onset: Typically 35-44 years (adult onset); juvenile form before age 20

approved_treatments.mechanism_correct: Inhibits vesicular monoamine transporter 2, reducing chorea (involuntary movements). It is SYMPTOMATIC ONLY — it does not modify disease progression or reduce mutant huntingtin.
approved_treatments.note: Symptomatic treatment for chorea. No disease-modifying therapy is yet approved for HD.

investigational: Antisense oligonucleotides (ASO) targeting HTT mRNA (tominersen/RG6042 — Phase 3 halted; others ongoing)

disease.human_summary: Huntington disease is an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder caused by a CAG repeat expansion in HTT. It causes progressive motor dysfunction (chorea), cognitive decline, and psychiatric symptoms, typically beginning in mid-adulthood. Mutant huntingtin forms toxic aggregates in striatal neurons. Current treatment is symptomatic only; allele-selective degradation and ASO silencing are the leading disease-modifying frontiers.
